svg.font-family: Segoe UI, Helvetica Neue, Arial, sans-serif
svg.text: One thruster, one column. The whole of B comes from this picture.
Where the thruster sits and which way it points is all the matrix knows — and it is all the matrix needs
the moment term is an arm
the line of action
the moment arm
the thruster
The check that makes the rule believable
r = (x, y) is the thruster position. With x = 1.2 m, y = 0.8 m and e
40° to port of the bow, x e_y − y e_x = −1.3842 and the arm
measures 1.3842 m. The third entry is not a new idea — it is the
ordinary force times perpendicular distance, sign included.
the rule
one newton from a thruster at (x, y) along e
that column depends on geometry alone
n thrusters, n columns
Forces add, so the columns sit side by side. No calibration,
no fitting, no measured data enters anywhere.
The base Otter, from the same rule
Both propellers face forward, so e = (1, 0), and they sit at
x = 0, y = ∓0.395 m, giving x e_y − y e_x = ±0.395.
e_y = 0 for both, so the middle row of B is empty.
e must be a unit vector
Entering (2, 0) instead of (1, 0) silently doubles that thruster's
authority, and every rank test still passes.
